opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I've always come at it is to ask what the right *inductive bias* is for a model that has to process a really long sequence. With attention, you get this very powerful mechanism where every token can look at every other token, but it comes at a cost. It's quadratic in the sequence length, and more fundamentally, it doesn't really compress anything. It keeps the entire history around in its cache. That works great up to a point, but if you want to scale to hundreds of thousands or millions of steps, or to modalities like raw audio or genomics where the sequences are naturally enormous, that starts to break down.

The alternative I've been interested in for a long time comes out of my PhD work on continuous-time memory. The question was: how can a model maintain a compressed representation of everything it's seen so far, online, as new inputs stream in? That led to things like HiPPO, which is a principled way of projecting the history of a signal onto a set of basis functions, and from there to structured state space models like S4. The idea is that you have a recurrent state that evolves according to a linear dynamical system. Because it's linear and structured, you can compute it very efficiently, either as a recurrence at inference time or as a convolution or parallel scan during training. So you get linear scaling in sequence length and constant memory per step when you're generating.

The challenge with those early models was that they were time-invariant: the dynamics were the same no matter what the input was. That's great for continuous signals like audio, but it struggled on information-dense discrete data like language, where you need to decide what to remember and what to throw away depending on the content. That was really the motivation for Mamba, where we made the state space parameters depend on the input. That's what we call selectivity. It lets the model choose, at each step, whether to absorb something into its state or ignore it. That turned out to be the key ingredient for closing a lot of the gap with Transformers on language.

So at a high level, I see it as a trade-off between two kinds of memory. Attention is like a perfect lookup table, and state space models are like a compressed, fuzzy summary. Each has strengths. Recurrent models are much more efficient and can in principle handle unbounded context, but they can have trouble with exact retrieval of some specific detail from far back. That's why a lot of the most practical systems now, and a lot of what I'm excited about, are hybrids that interleave a few attention layers with mostly SSM layers. You get most of the efficiency and still have the precise recall when you need it.

More broadly, I think long context isn't just about making the context window bigger. It's about building models that can actually *reason* over and compress information as they go, the way people do. We don't remember every word of a book, but we build up a useful state. Getting models to do that well is what I find most interesting.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is really the question that's driven a lot of my research for the past several years. The way I think about it is that long context is fundamentally a problem of memory and compression. When you're processing a sequence, you have to decide what to keep around from everything you've seen so far, and how to represent it so that it's useful later.

The transformer's answer is basically "keep everything." Attention stores the entire history as a cache of key-value pairs, and at every step you look back over all of it. That's incredibly powerful because you never have to commit to what matters ahead of time. But it also means the cost grows with the length of the sequence, quadratically during training and linearly per token at inference, and the memory footprint just keeps growing. So in some sense the transformer doesn't solve long context, it just pays for it.

The alternative lineage, which is where recurrent models and state space models live, is to maintain a fixed-size state. You compress the history into some vector or matrix, and you update it as new tokens come in. The appeal is obvious: constant memory, linear time, you can in principle run forever. The hard part is that compression is lossy, and for a long time these models just weren't good at deciding what to keep. The classic RNN would forget things, or the gradients would blow up, and the whole thing was hard to train.

So a lot of my work with S4 and then Mamba has been about making that compressed state actually good. With S4, the insight came from thinking about continuous-time signals and how to represent a function's history with a small set of coefficients, which gave us principled initializations and a way to train these things stably over very long ranges. Then with Mamba, the key piece was selectivity. The model gets to decide, as a function of the input, how much to let in and how much to forget. That sounds simple but it's the thing that lets a fixed-size state behave intelligently, where it can latch onto a relevant piece of information and hold it, or ignore filler tokens entirely.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that this isn't really an either-or. I think of attention and state space models as two points on a spectrum of how you trade off memory against expressivity. And in practice the hybrid architectures, where you have mostly recurrent layers with a few attention layers mixed in, tend to get most of the benefits of both. You get the efficiency of a compressed state for the bulk of the computation, and you keep a small amount of exact recall for the cases where you really need to retrieve something precisely.

So my honest approach is: figure out what the sequence model actually needs to remember, build the most efficient primitive that can do that, and then be pragmatic about combining it with other mechanisms where the primitive falls short.

astra-6.text:
I think the first thing is to distinguish between being able to process a long sequence and actually being able to use the information in it. You can make a model computationally efficient enough to accept a million tokens, but that doesn’t necessarily mean it can remember the particular thing you need from the beginning of that sequence.

The perspective we take with state space models is to think about a sequence as a dynamical system. As new inputs arrive, you update a state that summarizes the history. That gives you a way to process sequences with computation that scales linearly in their length, and at generation time you don’t have to keep the entire history around.

But then the central question becomes: what should that state remember? A fixed-size state is a compression of the past, so there’s a tradeoff. You want to retain information that will matter later without spending resources on everything you’ve seen. A lot of the work is about designing that update mechanism so the model can preserve information over long timescales and selectively incorporate new information.

So I’d approach long context as both an efficiency problem and a memory problem. You need an architecture that can afford to process the sequence, and you need to test whether it actually uses information across that sequence.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first question is what you want the model to do with that context. Being able to feed in a million tokens is different from being able to use all of that information effectively.

One way to think about it is as a memory problem. In a Transformer, you retain a representation of every token, and attention lets you look back at those representations. That’s a very flexible way to access the past, but the cost grows with the length of the sequence.

With a state space model, you instead maintain a state that summarizes the history. As each new input arrives, you update that state. That gives you a way to process very long sequences efficiently, but it creates a different challenge: what information should you remember, and what can you afford to forget?

So my approach is to look at both sides: can we build a computationally efficient mechanism for carrying information over long distances, and can the model learn to preserve the information that actually matters? You need both. An architecture can technically support a very long context without making effective use of it.
